newsitem.title: USA: Petrobras exec confident Brazil behind oil reforms.
newsitem.headline: Petrobras exec confident Brazil behind oil reforms.

text.p: Brazil's political environment has become more favorable for finalizing new regulations to open the oil industry, and should allow the process to be completed by the first half of 1997 at the latest, an official at state oil monopoly Petrobras said Monday.

"Optimists were saying the regulations would be approved by August. Now, the optimists say maybe by the end of the year. It all depends on the politics, but it should be by the first semester of 1997," Abrahao said.

Speaking at an oil industry conference in Miami, Dirceu Abrahao, Petrobras manager of new ventures, said recent results of municipal elections showed a lack of support for the Workers Party, one of the groups working to stymie the opening of the oil industry to foreign investment.
"President Cardosa gained a lot of support from the elections," said Abrahao, noting much "political adjustment" has to take place before 43 years of the Petrobras monopoly is altered.
Putting a timeframe for completing the regulations is made difficult by these political realities, and the by massive "cultural" changes underway within the Brazilian industry.

"New" regulation of the Brazilian oil industry is based a constitutional amendment issued in November 1995, under which contracts can be signed with foreign private or state-owned companies for oil and natural gas exploration, refining and import/export of oil and products, as well as for transportation and storage of oil and refined products.
The state will maintain the monopoly over the oil industry, and Petrobras will lose its power to administer state oil policy under the changes.
The government instead will form a National Petroleum Agency, charged with organizing tenders for bids, granting licenses for exploration and production and other activities.

Abrahao noted there are no plans to privatize Petrobras, as explained in the oil sector regulation package sent to the National Congress on July 5. Abrahao said once the regulations are prepared for congressional approval, he would like to discuss the rules with potential investors.
Already, Abrahao said more than 70 foreign companies have expressed interest in forming joint ventures, just waiting fo the regulation process to be finalized.
Overall, Petrobras has selected more than 200 projects for possible partnerships in order to enlarge resources capacity and increase technological capabilities.
Notable energy projects the government hopes to attract foreign oil money are the Bolivia-Brazil pipeline, the Urucu-Jurua gas project and the Argentina gas project, Abrahao said.
